title: Finding a Job That Actually Fits You
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham shares highlights from a WorkLife podcast conversation with executive recruiter Jamie Tilotta Green, prompted by a reader poll asking how to find a job that actually fits. The framing claim is that people approach job searches backward, worrying whether a company wants them rather than what they themselves need, and that fit has three parts: skills, culture and motivation, with motivation the one most often skipped. The three takeaways are to tell career stories with context, insight and result instead of reading the news of your resume, to treat interviews as a way to gather good data about what is hard in the role, and to listen when the vibes are off. The piece stresses authenticity throughout and includes practical interview questions such as the postmortem question about why the job might fail.
points: Fit has three parts, skills, culture and motivation, and motivation is the one candidates and companies most often ignore.
A strong career story needs a villain, meaning why the work was hard, plus the insight uncovered and the result.
Interviews are built to deliver good news, so the candidate should push past polished answers with repeated whys and a postmortem question.
Forcing a fit when something feels off usually means being back on the market in months, feeling worse.
quotes: Jamie breaks fit into three parts: skills, culture, and motivation. Motivation is the one everyone skips.
I think most of us approach job searches backward. We spend enormous energy figuring out whether a company wants us.
Interviews are built to give you good news. Your job is to get good data.
Use interviews to find what's hard, because that's the actual job.
If you dress up your skills, perform the culture, or fake the motivation, you might get the job. You won't get fit.
Jamie’s point is that forcing a fit doesn’t solve anything. You’ll be back on the market in six months, feeling worse.
Stop contorting yourself into a pretzel to get the offer. Companies can tell. Authenticity is attractive, and it’s what makes you the strongest hire.
